strengths: The paper extends the early directional convergence phenomenon from two-homogeneous neural networks (prior work [1]) to L-homogeneous networks with L>2, which requires a genuinely new proof technique (time rescaling by delta^(L-2)) since the constrained NCF gradient flow can now blow up in finite time (Lemma 5.2), unlike the L=2 case where it remains bounded. This is a nontrivial technical contribution clearly delineated from prior work in Section 5.1.1.

The theoretical results (Theorem 5.1, Lemma 5.2, Theorem 5.3, Lemma 5.4) are proven rigorously and in detail in the appendix, with careful tracking of epsilon-delta dependencies via Gronwall's inequality and KL-type arguments.

The paper is honest and clear about its limitations: it explicitly notes that Assumption 1 excludes ReLU networks, discusses the specific technical obstruction (lack of local Lipschitzness of the Clarke subdifferential dynamics) preventing extension to ReLU networks, and clearly states that Theorem 5.3 is limited to separable-structure networks, excluding fully connected networks.

Small-scale but illustrative experiments (squared-ReLU and ReLU toy networks) support the theoretical claims and additionally reveal an unexplained low-rank structure phenomenon, which is honestly flagged as unexplained by the theory and left for future work rather than overclaimed.
The related work section situates the contribution well relative to two-homogeneous directional convergence work, NTK/lazy-training regime, and margin-maximization literature.
weaknesses: The core assumption of locally Lipschitz gradients excludes the most practically relevant architecture (ReLU networks with depth >2), and the deep homogeneous networks it does cover (deep linear networks, powers of ReLU, polynomial activations) are of limited practical use; the significance of the contribution is thus mostly theoretical/foundational rather than broadly impactful.

The saddle-point result (Theorem 5.3) relies on a strong and somewhat opaque separability assumption (H = Hn + Hz) that explicitly excludes fully connected networks, substantially limiting its applicability; the paper acknowledges this but does not provide any concrete non-trivial example architecture (beyond generic decomposition) where this structure holds for deep networks.

The experiments are very small-scale (single toy problems, single random seeds it appears) and mainly serve as sanity checks/illustrations rather than a systematic empirical validation of the theory's predictions (e.g., no exploration of how tightness of bounds varies with L, depth, or initialization scale, no quantitative comparison of predicted vs actual epsilon/delta/T relationships).

The constants (delta-bar, T_epsilon, B_epsilon, K_epsilon, etc.) in the theorems are defined implicitly via existence and are not given explicit closed-form dependence on network width, depth, or data, making it hard to assess how small 'sufficiently small' initialization needs to be in practice or how the results scale with network size.

The paper explicitly leaves the emergence of low-rank structure in the weights unexplained, which is presented as a major empirically observed phenomenon but is outside the scope of the actual theoretical contribution, slightly overstating the completeness of the picture given by Theorem 5.1 relative to what is empirically shown in Section 5.1.2.

strengths: The paper is technically careful: it identifies a genuine new difficulty relative to the two-homogeneous case (the NCF gradient flow trajectory can now blow up in finite time rather than remaining bounded), and it works out how the unbounded Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality of Ji & Telgarsky can be adapted to handle this case (Lemma 5.2).

The time-rescaling argument (s(t) = w(t/\delta^{L-2})/\delta) is a reasonable and clearly explained mechanism for connecting the weight dynamics to the NCF dynamics for L>2, and the authors explicitly contrast it with the L=2 analysis in [1], showing they understand what changes and why.

The results cover both square and logistic loss, and extend the early-directional-convergence phenomenon to a directional convergence result near a restricted class of saddle points, mirroring analogous results in [1] but for deeper homogeneous networks.

The paper is reasonably honest about its own limitations: it explicitly flags that the results exclude ReLU networks, that the low-rank structure observed empirically is unexplained by the theory, and that the saddle-point result requires a separable (additive) architecture that excludes fully connected networks.

Toy experiments (squared-ReLU and ReLU) are provided that qualitatively support the theoretical claims and additionally suggest (without proof) that similar phenomena may hold beyond the theorem's stated assumptions (i.e., for ReLU networks).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution over [1] is fairly narrow: the authors themselves state that the “main conceptual innovation” is the time rescaling by delta^(L-2), and the overall proof strategy (compare weight dynamics to NCF gradient flow via Gronwall's inequality) is essentially the same template as in the two-homogeneous paper. This makes the contribution feel more like a technical extension than a substantially new insight.

The class of networks actually covered (locally Lipschitz gradient, L>2 homogeneous) explicitly excludes ReLU networks, which are the dominant practically relevant nonlinearity; the paper's own experiments show ReLU nets exhibit the same phenomenon, but the theory provides no guarantee for this important case, and the discussion of why the proof breaks down is only qualitative/informal (no concrete partial results or bounds).

The saddle-point result (Theorem 5.3) requires the network to have an additive/separable structure H(x;w) = H_n(x;w_n) + H_z(x;w_z), which the authors acknowledge excludes fully-connected deep networks entirely — arguably the setting motivating the whole line of work on saddle-to-saddle dynamics. This substantially limits the significance and applicability of the second main result.

Empirical validation is limited to small, synthetic teacher-student toy examples (random Gaussian teacher weights, uniform sphere inputs) with no realistic data, tasks, or architectures, and no experiments confirming the described early-time asymptotics quantitatively (e.g., verifying the T_\epsilon/\delta^{L-2} scaling or the sharpness of the bounds) beyond qualitative loss/norm plots.

The paper documents (via the low-rank structure observations in Section 5.1.2) a clear gap between what the theory explains and what is empirically observed, which somewhat undercuts the completeness/significance of the theoretical story being told — the directional convergence result alone does not capture much of what actually appears to be happening structurally in the weights.

The presentation is heavy with lengthy proof sketches and constant-tracking (Tϵ, Bϵ, Cϵ, etc.) in the main text, which could be moved to appendices to make room for deeper discussion of implications, comparison with alternative approaches, or more substantial experiments.

strengths: The paper makes a genuine technical advance by extending early directional convergence results from two-homogeneous networks (prior work [1]) to L-homogeneous networks with L>2, which requires new insight (the delta^{L-2} time-rescaling) since the associated NCF gradient flow can blow up in finite time, unlike the L=2 case. This is a non-trivial mathematical extension, not a routine generalization.

The theoretical development is rigorous: Theorem 5.1 and Theorem 5.3 are proven in detail via careful epsilon-delta arguments, Gronwall's inequality, and an unbounded Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality; supporting lemmas (KKT characterization of NCF critical points, boundedness/convergence dichotomy) are cleanly established.
The paper extends the analysis to saddle points under a separable-structure assumption, connecting to observed saddle-to-saddle training dynamics phenomena in the literature.

The authors are commendably transparent about limitations: they explicitly discuss why the locally-Lipschitz-gradient assumption excludes ReLU networks, explain the specific technical obstruction to extending the proof to non-differentiable networks, and clearly flag that the saddle-point result requires a separability assumption incompatible with fully-connected networks.

Toy experiments (squared-ReLU and even ReLU networks) empirically support the directional convergence claim and additionally surface an intriguing low-rank structure phenomenon in the weights, which the authors honestly acknowledge is not explained by their theory, providing a good direction for future work.
The related work section situates the contribution well within lazy/rich training regimes and saddle-to-saddle dynamics literature.
weaknesses: The core assumption of locally Lipschitz gradients excludes the most practically relevant case (ReLU networks), and the paper only provides an informal discussion plus small-scale empirical illustration for ReLU rather than any rigorous partial result, leaving the ReLU case entirely open.

The saddle-point result (Theorem 5.3) relies on a separable output structure H = H_n + H_z that explicitly excludes standard fully-connected deep architectures, substantially limiting its applicability; the authors acknowledge this but it remains a significant restriction on the generality of the second main contribution.

Empirical validation is limited to very small synthetic toy models (single random datasets, small width networks) rather than more realistic settings, so the practical relevance/generality of the theoretical predictions is only weakly demonstrated.

The observed low-rank structure in the weights during early training is an interesting empirical finding but is entirely unexplained by the theory, so the paper's explanatory power stops short of characterizing this seemingly important phenomenon.

The conceptual novelty relative to prior work [1] is somewhat narrow (primarily the time-rescaling by delta^{L-2} and handling of the finite-time blow-up of the NCF flow), which, combined with the restrictive assumptions, tempers the overall significance of the contribution despite its technical solidity.

strengths: Extends the early directional convergence phenomenon (previously known only for two-homogeneous/shallow networks) to deep L-homogeneous networks with L>2, which is a genuine technical advance requiring nontrivial new tools (time rescaling by delta^(L-2), handling gradient flow of the NCF that can blow up in finite time, use of the unbounded Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality).

The paper clearly delineates the conceptual novelty relative to Kumar & Haupt (2024), explaining precisely why L=2 and L>2 require different proof strategies (finite-time blow-up of NCF dynamics vs. bounded dynamics), which shows a mature understanding of the technical landscape.

The second contribution (necessary and sufficient conditions for rank-one KKT points of the constrained NCF for feed-forward networks with (Leaky) ReLU and polynomial (Leaky) ReLU activations) is a nice complementary structural result, giving insight into why low-rank structure emerges early in training, and is supported by clean theoretical characterizations (Theorems 3 and 4) plus a full proof.

Empirical validation is reasonably thorough for the scope of the claims: toy experiments illustrate the main theorem's predictions (Figure 1), and systematic numerical checks (Tables 1 and 2, Figure 3) validate the rank-one and non-negativity assumptions underlying Theorems 3 and 4 across multiple architectures, depths, and activation choices.

The paper is unusually candid about limitations: it explicitly flags the exclusion of non-differentiable (ReLU) networks from the main convergence theorem, and includes a dedicated appendix (Appendix D) explaining precisely why the proof technique breaks down for non-Lipschitz-gradient networks, which is commendable scientific honesty rather than a mere disclaimer.

The writing is generally clear, well-organized, and the proof sketches in the main text (Section 4.1.1) provide useful high-level intuition before diving into the lengthy formal appendix proofs, aiding reproducibility and readability.
weaknesses: The central assumption (locally Lipschitz gradients, homogeneity strictly greater than 2) excludes the most practically important case of ReLU networks entirely, which are arguably the primary motivation for studying 'early directional convergence' in the first place (as ReLU networks are the setting of the original Maennel et al. 2018 and much follow-up work). This significantly limits the practical relevance/significance of the main convergence theorem, since it primarily covers polynomial-ReLU or linear/monomial networks that are less commonly used in practice.

The two parts of the paper (Section 4 dynamical result and Section 5 static KKT characterization) are only loosely connected: Section 4 does not explain why gradient flow should converge specifically to rank-one KKT points, and Section 5's rank-one characterization is motivated only by empirical observation, with the connection between the two results left as an open question. This somewhat weakens the overall narrative cohesion and the paper reads as two separate contributions bundled together.

The necessary and sufficient conditions in Section 5 require restrictive additional assumptions (non-negativity of entries when alpha != 1, and a pre-supposed rank-one structure) that are justified only empirically (via a small set of random Gaussian training data experiments) rather than proven to hold generically or to characterize when gradient-based methods will find such KKT points; the theoretical guarantee that such assumptions hold is missing.

The experiments are fairly small-scale (single small synthetic examples, low-dimensional random Gaussian training data, small networks) and do not test practical/real-world settings, which limits how much the empirical validation strengthens the significance claims beyond a proof-of-concept.

The theoretical contribution, while technically solid, is fairly incremental in spirit relative to Kumar & Haupt (2024) -- the core proof strategy (comparing rescaled gradient flow with NCF gradient flow via Gronwall's inequality) is inherited from that prior work, with the main new ingredient being the time-rescaling trick and handling of finite-time blowup; the degree of conceptual novelty could be viewed as modest for some readers.

The paper does not discuss how the results might inform practical initialization strategies or training algorithms, nor connect the theoretical findings back to observed empirical phenomena in real deep networks (e.g., generalization benefits of small initialization), leaving the broader significance for the field somewhat implicit rather than concretely argued.

strengths: The extension of early directional convergence from two-homogeneous to deep (L>2)-homogeneous networks is technically non-trivial: the authors must handle gradient-flow trajectories of the neural correlation function (NCF) that can become unbounded in finite time (unlike the L=2 case), requiring new growth-rate estimates (e.g., the κ/(T*-t)^{1/(L-2)} lower bound) and a careful time-rescaling argument (by δ^{L-2}).

The proofs are detailed and appear internally consistent, making good use of the unbounded Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequality, Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions, and Gronwall's inequality; the paper is transparent about which technical machinery is borrowed from Ji & Telgarsky (2020) versus newly developed.

The second contribution (necessary and sufficient conditions for rank-one KKT points of the constrained NCF for Leaky ReLU and polynomial Leaky ReLU feed-forward networks) is a nice complement to the dynamical result, providing an explicit constructive/reductive characterization (reducing to a smaller optimization problem) that is validated with small-scale numerical experiments.

The paper is reasonably honest about its limitations, explicitly noting that the locally-Lipschitz-gradient assumption excludes ReLU networks, and includes an appendix discussing why extending the argument to non-smooth (ReLU) networks is technically difficult rather than glossing over this gap.

The writing includes helpful proof sketches and intuition (e.g., explaining why the gradient scales as δ^{L-1} and why rescaling time by δ^{L-2} is needed), which aids reproducibility of the theoretical arguments.
weaknesses: The central dynamical result excludes ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks (the most practically used homogeneous activations), restricting applicability to deep linear networks and polynomial/monomial activations that are rarely used in practice; this substantially limits the practical significance of Theorem 1, and the paper openly acknowledges this as an unresolved gap rather than a solved problem.

The theoretical novelty relative to Kumar & Haupt (2024) is somewhat incremental: the overall proof strategy (NCF, KKT points, directional convergence via KL-type arguments) is inherited wholesale, and the main new ingredient is the δ^{L-2} time-rescaling combined with handling finite-time blow-up of the NCF gradient flow — a natural but fairly narrow technical generalization.

Theorem 1's conclusion is a disjunction (either approximate convergence to a non-negative KKT point of the NCF, or the weights become vanishingly small), and the paper does not characterize which scenario occurs for a given initialization beyond noting it depends on w0 in an unspecified way; this limits the theorem's predictive/explanatory power for practitioners.

The necessary conditions in Section 5 for rank-one KKT points require an additional non-negativity assumption on hidden weight vectors that is not proven to hold in general but only verified numerically on small random instances (2-3 layers, small width, Gaussian synthetic data); the paper is candid about this but it means the 'necessary and sufficient' characterization is conditional rather than fully general.

The empirical validation throughout the paper (Figures 1-3, Tables 1-2) is confined to small toy/synthetic settings (single squared-ReLU example, small random two/three-layer networks with Gaussian inputs), with no experiments on realistic architectures, datasets, or an exploration of how the early-stage phenomenon connects to final trained-model behavior or generalization, which limits confidence in the broader significance of the findings.

The paper does not address why gradient descent/ascent empirically tends to converge to rank-one, non-negative KKT points rather than other (possibly higher-rank) KKT points of the non-convex NCF; this is explicitly left as future work, leaving the explanatory chain from 'early directional convergence' to 'observed structural properties of trained networks' incomplete.

strengths: Extends the early directional convergence phenomenon from two-homogeneous networks (Kumar & Haupt 2024) to deep L-homogeneous networks (L>2), addressing a clearly identified gap since prior rigorous work was confined to shallow/two-layer settings.

The extension is technically non-trivial: for L>2 the gradient flow of the neural correlation function can diverge to infinity in finite time (unlike the L=2 case), requiring new machinery (rate of blow-up bounds, unbounded KL inequality of Ji & Telgarsky) and a novel time-rescaling by δ^{L-2}; the authors clearly articulate this conceptual difference from prior work.

The second contribution—necessary and sufficient conditions for rank-one KKT points of the constrained NCF for feed-forward Leaky ReLU / polynomial Leaky ReLU networks—is a genuinely new structural characterization, with a clean reduction to a smaller optimization problem, and is well motivated by an empirical observation (Figure 1/2) that would otherwise be unexplained by Theorem 1 alone.

Theoretical claims are supported by careful, complete proofs (many pages of appendix), and empirical experiments (Tables 1-2, Figures 1-3) systematically validate the rank-one and non-negativity assumptions across multiple activation functions and layer depths, lending credibility to the sufficiency/necessity results.

The paper is transparent about limitations: it explicitly states the locally-Lipschitz-gradient assumption excludes ReLU, and includes an appendix (D) explaining precisely why the proof technique breaks down for non-smooth activations, which is an honest and useful discussion rather than a hidden gap.
Related work section is thorough and correctly situates the contribution relative to NTK/mean-field theories and prior shallow-network small-init analyses.
weaknesses: The core theory (Theorem 1) excludes ReLU networks, the most practically dominant architecture, and applies only to networks with locally Lipschitz gradients (deep linear, polynomial ReLU, monomial activations); this substantially limits the direct practical relevance of the main convergence result, even though the paper is upfront about this.

The rank-one KKT characterization in Section 5 is also restricted to fully-connected feed-forward architectures; there's no treatment of convolutional, residual, or attention architectures, which limits generality of the second contribution.

The central open question motivating Section 5 (why gradient descent/ascent empirically favors rank-one, non-negative KKT points among the many possible KKT points of the non-convex constrained NCF) is left completely unanswered; the paper provides characterization conditional on these assumptions being true rather than proving why they emerge, somewhat limiting the explanatory power of the results.

All numerical experiments use small-scale synthetic random Gaussian/uniform-sphere data (n=100, low dimension); there is no experiment connecting the early-training phenomenon to downstream generalization or to more realistic datasets/architectures, so the practical significance of the phenomenon remains illustrative rather than demonstrated at scale.

The necessary-and-sufficient conditions for α≠1 additionally require a non-negativity assumption on the alignment vectors that is itself only empirically (not theoretically) justified, which weakens the completeness of the characterization in that regime.

The paper's theoretical result concerns only the 'early stage' of training under vanishingly small initialization; it does not address how or whether this directional convergence connects to later-stage training dynamics or final generalization behavior, which is acknowledged as future work but limits the paper's standalone significance.
